summary: This memo defines two SMTP reply codes, 521 and 556. Code 521 was described in an Experimental RFC in 1995 and is widely used but never formally part of SMTP. Both let a server say it does not accept mail.

eli5.summary: When you try to send a mail to a place that never takes any, the server can say so clearly with a number. This defines two such numbers.

questions: what is a dummy smtp server
subtitle: Two SMTP reply codes that let a host say plainly: this machine does not accept mail at all.

tldr.problem: A host that runs no mail server makes senders wait for a connection timeout, then queue and retry the message for a long time before the originator hears about the failure.
tldr.mechanism: SMTP gains reply code 521, sent when a connection opens, and reply code 556, sent by a relay that already knows a destination domain takes no mail. Both are permanent failures.
tldr.outcome: The 521 code, already in wide use since an Experimental RFC in 1995, is now formally part of SMTP, and the 1995 experiment ends.

today: RFC 7504 is a Proposed Standard from June 2015. It updates RFC 1846 and RFC 5321 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Two New Reply Codes
sections.content:
RFC 7504 updates the list of reply codes in the SMTP specification (RFC 5321) with two new codes, 521 and 556. Both are used to indicate that an Internet host does not accept incoming mail at all.

The scope is narrow. The RFC says it does not apply when a host sometimes accepts mail but may reject particular messages, or even all messages, under specific circumstances.
sections.eli5: Two new numbers are added to the list of answers a mail computer can give. Both mean: this place never takes mail.

sections.title: Why a Clear Refusal Helps
sections.content:
Many Internet hosts cannot offer mail service for technical, operational or administrative reasons. If an SMTP client tries to open a mail connection to a system with no SMTP server, the attempt times out. SMTP requires that a timeout makes the client queue the message and retry for an extended period.

That wastes resources and delays the error message getting back to the originator. The RFC names two alternatives. One is a dummy SMTP server that answers every connection attempt with a fatal error reply code. The other is learning from a separate source, such as a DNS record, that the host does not receive mail. The two new codes serve those two cases.
sections.eli5: Knocking on a door where nobody lives takes forever to give up. A sign on the door saves everyone the waiting.

sections.title: Code 521: The Host Takes No Mail
sections.content:
Code 521 is reserved for connection-opening time. It replaces the usual 220 greeting to say the host does not accept mail under any circumstances. It SHOULD be used by dummy SMTP servers whose sole purpose is to tell connecting systems that the host never accepts mail. It MAY be used in other situations with the same intent.

It SHOULD NOT be used when a server rejects mail from particular hosts or addresses, or when mail for a particular destination host is not accepted. Reply code 554 is more appropriate for most of those cases. A message such as "Server does not accept mail" is acceptable text to accompany it.

After a 521 replaces the 220, the SMTP session proceeds normally. If the client sends commands other than QUIT, the server MAY keep sending 521 replies or simply close the connection. If the point of the dummy server is to conserve resources, closing is usually preferable.
sections.eli5: When you knock, the first thing you hear is: we never take mail here. If you keep knocking, the house can repeat itself or just close the door.

sections.title: Code 556: The Domain Takes No Mail
sections.content:
Code 556 is for intermediate systems, typically relays. Suppose a relay would normally open a connection to the host named in a forward-pointing address, but it can tell without trying that the host does not accept mail. It then returns a 556 to the system that sent it the message. The one standardized way to know this, at the time of writing, is a special DNS record found during a lookup tied to a RCPT command, the null MX convention from RFC 7505.

When a server returns 556 after a command such as RCPT, the client treats it like any other permanent negative completion reply to that command. This is consistent with existing SMTP.
sections.eli5: A post office worker looks up the address in a directory, sees it says no mail accepted, and tells you straight away instead of trying to deliver.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 5321 and the Old Experiment
sections.content:
The RFC adds 521 with the message "Host does not accept mail" and 556 with the message "Domain does not accept mail" to the function group and numerical lists in Sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.3 of RFC 5321. It also places 521 in the "CONNECTION ESTABLISHMENT" part of Section 4.3.2, before 554, and 556 in the "RCPT" part of that section.

The 521 code was first formally proposed in the Experimental RFC 1846. By formalizing it, RFC 7504 ends that experiment. The general strategies for hosts that do not accept mail directly, discussed in RFC 1846, are out of scope here.
sections.eli5: The official rulebook gets two new lines, and an old trial run of one of them is declared finished.

sections.title: IANA and Security Notes
sections.content:
There is no registry of reply codes itself. IANA updated the "Enumerated Status Codes" subregistry of the SMTP Enhanced Status Codes Registry. It added 521 to the codes tied to enhanced code X.3.2, and added this document to the references for enhanced code X.1.10 and reply code 556.

For security, running no SMTP server, or one that only emits fixed strings, should give far fewer opportunities for problems than a full implementation. The specific codes tell the client more than a generic 5yz code but should have no other effect on security.
sections.eli5: The official list of codes gets updated, and a mail door that only says one sentence is harder to trick than a full-service desk.
